channel.title: Inside Desk
channel.description: A twice-daily brief on markets, geo-economics, politics, psychology and ordinary life. Optimistic by habit. Data first. Commentary, not advice.

item.title: The barrel and the screen
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The futures screen says the oil shock is cooling. The cargo market says it is still here. Only one of them has to be delivered by Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The futures screen says the oil shock is cooling. The cargo market says it is still here. Only one of them has to be delivered by Tuesday.

There are two oil prices this week, and they are not having the same week.

The first lives on the screen. Brent futures for December delivery settled on Thursday at $105.92 a barrel, fourteen cents lower on the day, and were trading at $105.14 late on Friday morning, European time4,3. That is the number on the evening news, the one that moves in cents and gets a verb: eased, edged, steadied.

The second lives in the tank. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Europe Brent spot price, a physical barrel loaded at the North Sea, was $126.55 on Wednesday, the latest day published1. Different instruments, a day apart, so do not subtract them to the cent. But a gap of roughly twenty dollars between the barrel you can load now and the barrel you can load in December is not a rounding error. It is the market telling you, in cash, what the present costs compared with the future it hopes for.

What the gap is made of. The present is expensive because the corridor is narrow. About 12.6 million barrels a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz on 13 October, according to Kpler data cited by BBC Verify, down from about 15 million at the end of September and against a pre-war baseline of roughly 17 million5. Attack reports to the UK’s maritime trade agency hit a weekly record of twelve between 5 and 11 October5. A December contract can price a negotiated reopening. A refinery that needs crude next week cannot run on a negotiation.

Why WTI is the tell. On the same Wednesday, EIA’s WTI spot, the American inland barrel at Cushing, was $101.91: $24.64 below Brent spot1,2. From July 2025 to the last trading day of February that gap averaged $4.29, on the desk’s arithmetic from the same EIA series; it peaked at $37.62 on 2 October. This is geography arriving as a price. A barrel in Oklahoma is a long way from a minefield. A barrel priced off the North Sea competes for the same European and Asian buyers who lost Gulf supply. This week WTI futures rose 5.6% while Brent rose 0.4%, helped by a large U.S. crude stock draw after hurricane-related production shut-ins3. The American barrel has its own weather.

Who pays the screen, and who pays the tank. Funds and hedgers trade the screen. Refiners, airlines, hauliers and anyone heating a house with oil pay something closer to the tank, with a lag. That is why the morning headline can say “oil eases” while your diesel invoice does not. European diesel refining margins fell almost 2% on Friday, to $78.67 a barrel, after the International Energy Agency agreed to release more diesel. In September they were as high as $953. Lower is not low.

The constructive read, and it is allowed. The screen is not lying; it is forecasting. A much cheaper December says the market expects the corridor to widen, through escorts, deals or plain adaptation. Brent spot has already come down from its 2026 peak of $138.21 on 7 April1. Emergency stocks are being released, and the IEA says total releases will exceed the 400 million barrels pledged in March6. The honest position is to hold both prices in your head at once: the future is priced as calmer, the present is not, and you live in the present first.

What the desk will not do is pretend the screen is the barrel. When the two prices converge it will be because tankers are moving, or because demand has been destroyed. Those are very different Tuesdays. The spot assessment, not the headline verb, will tell you which one arrived.

Sources

  1. Crude Oil Prices: Brent – Europe (DCOILBRENTEU), EIA spot price — U.S. EIA via FRED, St. Louis Fed
  2. Crude Oil Prices: West Texas Intermediate – Cushing (DCOILWTICO) — U.S. EIA via FRED, St. Louis Fed
  3. Oil eases but heads for small weekly gain as investors focus on Middle East supply — Reuters, via CNBC
  4. Brent steady as US weighs easing shadow fleet sanctions — Reuters, via The Star
  5. Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow — BBC Verify
  6. IEA Governing Board statement on energy markets and security — International Energy Agency

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: a 100-million-barrel answer to a 4.4-million-barrel-a-day question
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The IEA's statement is accurate. The arithmetic is simply less comforting than the adjectives.
item.content:encoded:
The IEA's statement is accurate. The arithmetic is simply less comforting than the adjectives.

The podium, in its own words. On Thursday the IEA’s Governing Board said about 330 million barrels had been released under the March collective action, that roughly 100 million barrels remain, and that total releases will exceed the original 400 million because some members have given more than they pledged1. It promised over 20 million barrels of diesel “as soon as possible”1. Nothing in that statement is false.

The print. Kpler data cited by BBC Verify put Hormuz flows at about 12.6 million barrels a day on 13 October, against a pre-war baseline of roughly 17 million2. That is a hole of about 4.4 million barrels, every day.

Same units, please. G7 leaders set a four-month deadline on 2 October for releasing the outstanding 100 million barrels, according to S&P Global’s Platts3. Spread over four months, about 122 days, that is roughly 0.8 million barrels a day: under a fifth of today’s gap. Released faster, it helps more for less long. Either way it is a bridge, not a pipeline.

The cushion is real. On 7 October the IEA said member governments still hold around 1.1 billion barrels of public emergency stocks, including over 200 million barrels of diesel4. Divide that by today’s gap and you get about eight months, on the desk’s arithmetic, before subtracting the barrels no government would ever leave itself without. Months, not weeks. That is the constructive half of the story, and it is true.

Verdict. The podium is accurate and insufficient, which is the normal condition of podiums. Releases buy time for the corridor to reopen; they do not reopen it. The market noticed, politely: European diesel margins slipped almost 2% on Friday, and one analyst quoted by Reuters said the release is unlikely to ease diesel tightness5.

Sources

  1. IEA Governing Board statement on energy markets and security — International Energy Agency
  2. Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow — BBC Verify
  3. IEA accelerates oil stock release, plans over 20 mil barrels of diesel — S&P Global Commodity Insights (Platts)
  4. Statement by IEA Executive Director on meeting of IEA Member governments on 7 October 2026 — International Energy Agency
  5. Oil eases but heads for small weekly gain as investors focus on Middle East supply — Reuters, via CNBC
  6. IEA to speed up oil stocks release including over 20 million barrels of diesel — Reuters, via MarketScreener

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The committee is behind the print, on purpose
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Euro-area inflation is 3.8%. The deposit rate is 2.5%. That gap is not negligence. It is a bet that wages stay calm.
item.content:encoded:
Euro-area inflation is 3.8%. The deposit rate is 2.5%. That gap is not negligence. It is a bet that wages stay calm.

Eurostat confirmed this morning that euro-area inflation was 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August1. Energy prices were 18.9% higher than a year earlier. Strip out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco and the rate was 2.5%; services ran at 3.2%1.

The ECB’s deposit rate is 2.50%, after increases that took effect in June and September2. Against headline inflation, that is a real rate of about minus 1.3 points. If you think the committee is asleep, read what it says it is doing.

“We do not react to energy prices, we react if we see risks of higher energy prices becoming embedded in inflation,” Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament’s economic committee on 28 September3. Her evidence that it is not yet embedded: compensation per employee grew 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first, and most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stand at around 2%3. And a quieter argument: long-term interest rates “have risen notably”, which she said will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than the September projections assumed3. The bond market is doing some of the committee’s work for it.

That is a coherent position, and also a bet. It holds as long as two dull prints stay dull: wages and core. Core edged up from 2.4% to 2.5% in September1. Not a break; a lean. The next decision is on 29 October4. The desk will be reading the wage line before the press conference, not after.

Sources

  1. HICP – monthly data, annual rate of change (prc_hicp_minr), September 2026 final — Eurostat
  2. Deposit facility rate (FM.D.U2.EUR.4F.KR.DFR.LEV) — ECB Data Portal
  3. Hearing of the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs of the European Parliament (speech by Christine Lagarde) — European Central Bank
  4. Meetings of the Governing Council and the General Council — European Central Bank

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The pump is the honest print
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Inflation is 3.8% on average. Nobody lives on the average. Which pipe comes into your house decides your year.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation is 3.8% on average. Nobody lives on the average. Which pipe comes into your house decides your year.

Averages are for committees. Households live inside categories, and Eurostat’s September detail shows how unevenly this shock lands1.

Liquid fuels and fuels for transport (petrol, diesel, heating oil) cost 33.8% more across the euro area than a year earlier. In Germany the same category was up 37.3%, from 27.5% in August1. Electricity, gas, solid fuels and heat, by contrast, were up 6.9% for the euro area. Everything outside energy, food, alcohol and tobacco: 2.5%1. German headline inflation on the harmonised measure was 3.3%, up from 2.9%1.

So two neighbours on the same street can be living in different inflation rates. The one who commutes by diesel and heats with oil sits near the top line of that chart. The one on a fixed electricity tariff who takes the train sits near the bottom. The headline 3.8% describes neither of them precisely.

The constructive part is that this is legible. Fuel is the part of the bill that reacts fastest to the screen in today’s lead piece: up first, and eventually down first. Grid tariffs and gas contracts move more slowly, in both directions. If you are deciding when to fill a heating-oil tank, which tariff to sign, or how to argue for a travel allowance, you need your category, not the average. That is information, not advice. Your contract and your local prices are the binding numbers.

Sources

  1. HICP – monthly data, annual rate of change (prc_hicp_minr): FUEL, ELC_GAS, TOT_X_NRG_FOOD, TOTAL; euro area and Germany — Eurostat
  2. Weekly Oil Bulletin — European Commission

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Keeping the night boring is now a convoy schedule
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Escorted transits are up, attacks are up, and both are true at once. The strait has become an operations problem, and operations can be counted.
item.content:encoded:
Escorted transits are up, attacks are up, and both are true at once. The strait has become an operations problem, and operations can be counted.

Attack reports to the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reached a weekly record of twelve between 5 and 11 October, according to a BBC Verify count; six came on a single day, Sunday the 11th1. Energy Intelligence, working from the same UKMTO reports, counts 26 commercial vessels attacked in the area from 1 to 14 October2.

At the same time, US Navy data indicate that the number of vessels given assistance through the strait in the first ten days of October was up 85% on the same period in August1. US Central Command says commercial traffic “continues to flow” with co-ordinated protection1. Both statements can be true. More ships are being protected, and more are being hit.

The losses are no longer only cargo. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after being struck by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday; its 21 crew were evacuated1. CNN reported two cargo ships sinking near the strait within 24 hours and, citing IMO data, called them only the second and third ships to sink in the Middle East since the war began in February3. Two seafarers from the tanker Petro Dolphin, hit near Oman’s Sohar anchorage, were still missing according to an Indian seafarers’ union1.

Iran says the shuttle route that tankers use near Oman’s coast is “unauthorised” and insists that vessels sail closer to its own shore1. That is the dispute in one line: not whether ships move, but whose lane they move in.

No chart today. A count of incident reports, compiled by different outlets on different date rules, is not yet a series worth drawing. When there is a consistent public dataset, the desk will draw it.

Sources

  1. Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow — BBC Verify
  2. Hormuz Attacks Hit Crude Flows, Testing Even Risk-Tolerant Shippers — Energy Intelligence
  3. Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks — CNN

Commentary for information only. Not advice.
